Today, unemployment among recent college graduates has risen to levels that should concern all of us. Many of the occupations most vulnerable to generative AI are the very white-collar, entry-level jobs that have long served as the first rung on the career ladder – jobs in business, finance, marketing, software development, customer support, and other knowledge professions.

Right now, the honest answer is that we don’t know nearly enough. Congress has remarkably little visibility into how AI is affecting hiring, wages, productivity, or job displacement across the economy. We’re debating one of the most consequential technological transformations in history with surprisingly little real-time data.

Artificial intelligence is one of the defining national security challenges of our time, and I welcome the administration recognizing that this technology requires serious, sustained attention at the highest levels of government. But creating a new title is not a substitute for having a coherent strategy. So far, the administration has resisted meaningful safeguards without offering a serious alternative for addressing the national security risks posed by increasingly powerful AI systems.
